reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The 39-39 projection is loud, but the Statcast profile explains exactly how it's possible. His 12.5% barrel rate and 48.4% hard-hit rate say the raw power is already translating at the big-league level, and his 11.9% walk rate says he's earning enough plate appearances to let it play. The one genuine fault line is a 34.3% chase rate that runs well below average, which keeps his xBA at .250 even as his xwOBA sits at .359 — he produces elite damage on contact while giving the zone away too often, and if pitchers ever fully commit to that, the at-bat quality could erode faster than the power numbers suggest. Add 29.5 ft/s sprint speed and you get a profile where the speed and the thump are both real, and the only question is whether the plate discipline ever tightens to let the contact component match everything else.

reports.name: Jordan Walker

The whole profile hinges on whether he can ever tighten the zone, because a 35.9% chase rate and a 30.7% whiff rate are the only reason a guy with this kind of contact quality isn't a perennial MVP candidate. reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The .407 xwOBA and 2.72 xERA living in the same body is the whole argument. At the plate, 16.5% barrel rate and 13.7% walk rate do the damage, and the strikeouts (23.3% K%) are the one real cost; a 30.7% whiff rate says pitchers have found something to exploit, but his discipline at the zone edge keeps the walks coming and the damage rate elite. On the mound, a 98.1 mph fastball with 2488 rpm and a 30.4% whiff rate against hitters produces a xERA that would anchor a rotation, not merely contribute to one. The projection of .285/.388/.547 with 38 home runs in 691 plate appearances is what you write down when everything holds, and the only real dependency is innings, because the question with Ohtani has never been talent.

reports.name: Jackson Merrill
reports.published_report: The power-speed combination here is the argument, but plate discipline is the wall he keeps running into. A 46.6% hard-hit rate and 29.0 ft/s sprint speed are both genuine weapons, and at 23 he projects to 26 home runs and 27 stolen bases across 667 plate appearances — that kind of dual threat is rare at this age. The problem is a 37.2% chase rate that drags his walk rate to 6.3% and keeps the OBP pinned at .292 despite an xSLG of .465 that says the contact quality delivers when he does connect. Bring the chase rate down and the underlying contact turns him into a true middle-of-the-order force; leave it where it is, and he's a volatile, exciting second-division regular who makes pitchers' lives easy in two-strike counts.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The contact metrics and the raw power read like a superstar; the strikeout rate is where the whole argument lives. De La Cruz runs a 93.8 mph average exit velocity that ranks at the 98th percentile, with a 13.8% barrel rate and 51.0% hard-hit rate to match, yet a 28.3% whiff rate drags his actual production back toward very good rather than transcendent. The .359 xwOBA says the underlying quality of contact is genuine, and a 10.7% walk rate means he's not completely exposed when pitchers work around him, so the projection's .811 OPS across 641 PA is a reasonable translation of what a high-strikeout, high-damage profile actually produces over a full season. Add 29 projected steals and the profile is a legitimate 26 HR shortstop who scores 95 runs, and the ceiling climbs sharply if that whiff rate comes down even a few points.

reports.name: CJ Abrams
reports.published_report: The 34-home-run projection is the headline, but the Statcast profile underneath it asks you to squint a little. His xSLG sits at .444, which is well short of the .512 the projection carries — the gap lives in his speed, his park, and the assumption that his contact quality trends forward rather than flat. A 37.1% chase rate and 28.9% whiff rate are genuine drag on the profile, and the fact that his xwOBA (72nd percentile) runs meaningfully ahead of both his contact rates and his raw exit velocity tells you the power is coming from barrel efficiency and legs, not brute force. If the plate discipline holds where it is, you're looking at a productive everyday shortstop who steals 32 bases and posts an .860 OPS; if pitchers tighten up the chase, the strikeout rate climbs and the OBP erodes first.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.1 ERA and a 0.6 WHIP at Double-A aren't numbers that need context — they're the argument. Anderson has struck out 135 batters against 13 walks across 93.3 innings at AA this season, and the command profile translates cleanly: a BB/9 of 2.0 in MLB terms, well below the 3.2 figure where most pitchers land, with a K-BB% that comes out to 21.9% against an average of 13.5%. The whole thing hinges on whether the stuff backs up the control at the highest level, because a left-hander this young who misses this many bats while almost never missing the zone has no obvious developmental ceiling short of a frontline starter. If the stuff softens in the jump, he's still a useful mid-rotation arm, but nothing in this line suggests you should expect softening.

reports.name: Zach Neto
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is a study in contradictions that collapse into one real problem: a 37.4% chase rate and 33.2% whiff rate that together produce a 30.6% strikeout rate, bottoming out at the 7th percentile. The barrel rate is genuine, 11.6% at the 76th percentile, and that carry shows up in the projection's 27 home runs across 707 plate appearances. But the xBA sits at .208, because barrels don't help you when you're swinging through pitches outside the zone at that frequency, and the .237 projected average reflects exactly that gap between raw contact quality and actual contact rate. If pitchers keep attacking him early in counts and he keeps biting, the power becomes a secondary story to a strikeout problem that makes him difficult to run out at shortstop every day; if he ever tightens the zone even modestly, the barrel rate and 23 projected steals make him a genuine multi-category contributor.

reports.name: Bo Bichette
reports.published_report: The 88th-percentile xBA tells the Bichette story better than any counting stat: he squares the ball up consistently, but a 41.1% chase rate keeps the walks near the floor and caps how much that contact quality compounds. The projection's .315 OBP on a .279 xBA isn't a contradiction — it's exactly what happens when a hitter puts wood on pitches outside the zone but can't work counts. A league-average shortstop, nothing more, useful enough to start but not a piece you build around.

The projection's .302 average with 29 stolen bases across 682 plate appearances is the natural extension of that profile, speed layered on top of a bat that simply doesn't give away outs. reports.name: Luis Arraez
reports.published_report: The whole argument is a .290 xBA at the 96th percentile sitting on top of a 1.2% barrel rate at the 2nd. Arraez doesn't hit the ball hard, full stop: 86.6 mph average exit velocity, 19.8% hard-hit rate, both scraping the bottom of the league. What he does instead is make contact at a rate that has almost no peer, a 4.4% strikeout rate and 7.9% whiff rate both at the 100th percentile, and he places the ball where fielders aren't, which is why the xBA and the actual projected average of .318 both look believable despite the soft contact. The profile hinges entirely on that contact skill holding; if his bat-to-ball ability erodes even slightly, there's no power floor to catch him, and that .788 projected OPS evaporates fast. Right now though, he's a .318 hitter who fields well by OAA (98th percentile) and beats his xwOBA by running into gaps, which is a real thing some hitters do and he does it as well as anyone.

At 19, posting a 15% strikeout rate at AA with 73 strikeouts in 495 plate appearances, Jesús Made is doing something most teenagers can't sniff at that level, and the MLB translation puts his K% at 18.4, well below where the average big-leaguer lands at 22.0. The speed is loud too: 33 stolen bases at AA this season, which pairs with the .272 average to sketch out a real on-base weapon if the walks ever catch up to the strikeout discipline. The ISO translates to .13 at the MLB level, a tick below average, so he's a contact-and-speed profile right now, not a power one, and whether he grows into a true everyday shortstop or settles into a high-contact utility role depends almost entirely on whether the gap power develops as he fills out.

reports.name: Ryan Sloan
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole read. Fourteen walks in 86.7 innings at AA translates to a 2.2 BB/9 when the MLB average sits at 3.2, and that gap is what makes Ryan Sloan worth tracking at 20 years old. His strikeout stuff is fine, 111 punchouts and 11.5 per nine at the level translating to roughly league-average swing-and-miss in the majors, but the command is the separator, sitting at the 99th percentile among pitchers in this pool. If the stuff holds its shape as he climbs, you're looking at a back-end starter who doesn't beat himself; if the velo or movement flattens out in the upper minors, the floor is depth arm and the walk rate becomes context rather than a calling card.

reports.name: Willi Castro
reports.published_report: The .261 projection with 18 home runs is doing a lot of heavy lifting for a profile that Statcast doesn't really trust. His xBA sits at .235 and his xwOBA at .309, both well below league average, with a 37.4% chase rate that explains almost everything. The 8.5% barrel rate is the one honest bright spot, suggesting the power can show up when he makes contact, but a 27.1% strikeout rate on that much swing-and-miss against pitches outside the zone means the contact comes infrequently enough to drag the whole line down. At 28.2 ft/s he's a genuine base-running asset and the positional flexibility across 2B and OF keeps him rostered, but if the chase rate doesn't come down this is a low-end regular carrying a counting-stat illusion propped up by Coors Field.

reports.name: Oneil Cruz
reports.published_report: The exit velocity is 95.7 mph and every ball he squares up is a problem — 17.5% barrel rate, 58.0% hard-hit, an xSLG of .493 that says the projection's .468 SLG is, if anything, conservative. That's the upside. The downside is a 36.9% whiff rate that lands at the first percentile, and a 35.3% strikeout rate to match, which means the xBA sits at .252 despite all that raw violence because he simply misses too often to run a real batting average. The whole profile hinges on whether he can make enough contact to keep pitchers from burying him: if the contact rate holds where it is, he's a 21-homer, 28-steal middle-of-the-order piece who never quite hits for average; if pitchers find the hole more reliably, the strikeouts swallow the rest.

reports.name: Shane McClanahan
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile and the projection are telling two different stories right now. A 4.14 xERA at the 46th percentile is not the McClanahan who was pitching like a Cy Young contender before the elbow, and a 22.3% strikeout rate that sits dead at league average explains why the underlying numbers look so ordinary. The fastball is still 95.6 mph, and a 27.0% whiff rate suggests the bat-missing ability hasn't fully evaporated. reports.name: Bryson Stott
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .268 against a current projection of .258, which tells you most of what you need to know: the bat-to-ball skills are quietly better than the surface numbers suggest. His 18.8% whiff rate and 16.6% strikeout rate are both well above average for a middle infielder, and paired with a 10.1% walk rate, the plate discipline profile is legitimately clean. The power ceiling is the honest constraint — a 5.9% barrel rate and 38.3% hard-hit rate translate to a guy who earns his 11 projected home runs rather than hitting them with authority, and the .402 projected SLG reflects that ceiling accurately. Where he separates himself is the full package: 27 projected steals, 96th-percentile fielding, and enough on-base capacity to function as a genuine everyday second baseman rather than one propped up by a favorable ballpark.

reports.name: Hunter Brown

That tension is the reason the projection sits at a 3.58 ERA over only 108.7 innings rather than reading like a mid-rotation anchor. reports.name: Luke Adams
reports.published_report: The contact-and-discipline combination here is what makes Luke Adams worth the conversation. At AAA in 264 plate appearances, he's struck out just 37 times against 35 walks, a 14% K-rate that translates to 18.1% at the MLB level while most hitters are sitting at 22.0%, and the walk rate follows him at 10.6% against an 8.5% norm. The ISO of .251 at AAA carries down to .179 in translation, real power for a hitter who also puts the ball in play at this rate, and with a .244 BABIP sitting underneath a .251 average, there's contact quality he isn't yet getting credit for. The profile hinges entirely on whether that BABIP recovers at a corner with no defensive value, because a first baseman who doesn't hit for a true average is just a bench piece waiting for a roster crunch.

reports.name: Lawrence Butler
reports.published_report: The walk rate is doing a lot of heavy lifting here. Butler's 11.9% BB% sits in the 81st percentile, and his 24.8% chase rate matches it — he genuinely knows the strike zone. The problem is what happens when pitchers find it: a 27.2% whiff rate and a 25.5% K% both land in the bottom quarter of the league, and the .235 xBA says the contact he does make isn't finding ground. Hard-hit rate at 45.1% is legitimately loud, but it's getting suppressed into a .373 xSLG by a barrel rate that's dead average, which means the projection's .226 AVG and .691 OPS aren't pessimism, they're just the math. If the plate discipline ever forces pitchers into enough mistake pitches to let the hard contact breathe, he's a useful regular with speed and a real on-base skill; if the strikeout rate stays where Statcast sees it, he's a patient bench outfielder on a large sample.

reports.name: Dylan Cease
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the one thing standing between Cease and a true ace conversation. His 36.1% strikeout rate sits at the 99th percentile, his 34.8% whiff rate isn't far behind, and hitters are averaging 86.0 mph exit velocity off him — the contact suppression is deep and consistent, not surface-level. But an 11.1% walk rate at the 19th percentile means he's handing back some of what he earns, and the projection reflects that tension: a 2.55 ERA over 179.0 innings with a 1.08 WHIP is an excellent season, not a Cy Young one. If the command tightens, the strikeout-to-contact profile here points somewhere rarefied; if it doesn't, he remains exactly what he is, a frontline arm who occasionally beats himself.

reports.name: Ronald Acuña Jr.
reports.published_report: The xwOBA is .360 and the xSLG is .470, yet the projection has him at .241 with 18 home runs across 481 plate appearances — that gap is the whole read. Acuña's quality-of-contact profile still belongs to a star: a 12.4% barrel rate, a 12.4% walk rate, and expected numbers that would look normal on a healthy, peak version of him. What the statcast card also shows is a 30.0% whiff rate sitting near the bottom of the league, which is what keeps the actual average suppressed and the projection conservative despite the underlying power, and a sprint speed of 27.0 ft/s that explains why the 23 projected steals represent a significant step back from what he once did on the bases. If the knee is right and the whiff rate retreats, the contact translates and this projection undersells him badly; if it doesn't, .241/.346/.424 is what you get, a useful walk-heavy outfielder who hits the ball hard enough to matter but no longer changes a roster the way he once did.

reports.name: Caleb Durbin
reports.published_report:
The Statcast profile is almost entirely contact-skill illusion: a 15.8% whiff rate and 13.3% strikeout rate that grade well above average, wrapped around an 83.6 mph average exit velocity that sits at the 1st percentile. He makes contact, constantly, softly. The .285 xwOBA and .319 xSLG are the honest translation of what that contact actually produces, and neither number suggests a regular third baseman.

Where the profile breathes is in the projection's 21 steals, the strikeout suppression, and the 88th-percentile fielding, which together sketch a useful player if Boston leans into the speed-and-glove version rather than waiting on power that the contact shape won't deliver. If the exit velocity doesn't climb, the .255/.325/.398 projection line is probably a ceiling, not a floor — and a second-division regular is the honest ceiling here.

Across AAA & AA this season, 30 walks in 94.4 innings translates to a BB/9 of 3.1 at the MLB equivalent, virtually identical to the 3.2 pitchers run on average, and the WHIP of 1.1 is the spine of a 3.7 ERA that grades out cleanly against the competition. The K-BB% of 20% across those levels translates to 14.5% in MLB terms, a tick above the league mean, which means the profile isn't built on strikeouts he doesn't quite own, his 10.0 K/9 in the minors comes back to 8.6 in translation, it's built on not giving hitters free passes. If the command holds in full-time big-league exposure, he's a multi-inning reliever with a real job; if it slips, 105 strikeouts don't leave enough margin to survive, and you're looking at a depth arm filling innings when someone goes down.

reports.name: Emerson Hancock
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the one thing keeping this profile afloat. At 5.9%, Hancock sits in the 89th percentile in BB%, and that control is doing real work against a Whiff rate of 23.7% and a Chase rate of 28.4% that don't generate many swing-and-miss events on their own. Hitters make contact, and when they do, 41.6% of it is hard — the xERA of 3.86 says the current run prevention is running a bit ahead of what the contact quality suggests. If the command holds, 165 projected innings and a 3.54 ERA make him a back-end starter worth rostering; if hitters start squaring up the fastball more consistently, the hard-hit numbers turn into a real ERA problem and he's relieving.

A 13% walk rate at AAA translates to 10.7% at the MLB level, which clears the 8.5% MLB average comfortably, so the on-base skills that make the speed usable are genuine. reports.name: Seiya Suzuki
reports.published_report: His chase rate sits at the 88th percentile and his walk rate is 12.1%, yet he strikes out 25.6% of the time, which is where the profile gets complicated. The discipline is genuine, but the whiff rate (24.6%) is median, and his average exit velocity of 88.4 mph doesn't do the power-side heavy lifting — his 10.4% barrel rate does. The .333 xwOBA and 27 projected home runs are credible precisely because he finds the barrel often enough to compensate for not hitting the ball especially hard. If the strikeout rate drifts higher, the .358 projected OBP still carries him; if it compresses, he becomes one of the more complete middle-of-the-order bats in the National League.

reports.name: Javier Sanoja
reports.published_report: An 8.3% strikeout rate that ranks in the 100th percentile tells you exactly what kind of hitter Sanoja is: contact-first, bat-to-ball, rarely punished by the swing-and-miss game. The problem is the power side of the ledger, where a 2.2% barrel rate and 86.7 mph average exit velocity leave almost no margin for damage, and an xSLG of .328 signals that the projection's .415 SLG is counting on contact volume to paper over genuine pop limitations. His 38.9% chase rate is the real hinge — a hitter this light on power needs to punish hittable pitches, and if pitchers learn to expand the zone without consequence, the contact skill stops carrying the profile. Either the floor here is a useful bench piece whose bat-to-ball keeps him employed, or the chase and exit velo numbers converge to make him easy to pitch around at the big-league level.

reports.name: Eduardo Quintero
reports.published_report: The .447 OBP at A+ is the headline, but the translation is where this profile gets complicated. Eduardo Quintero is drawing 81 walks in 456 plate appearances at A+ while hitting .310 with 42 stolen bases, a player who looks like a future leadoff centerfielder until you run the numbers through a level converter. The walk rate translates to 12.7% at the MLB level, comfortably above league average, but the ISO shrinks from .183 to .132, below the MLB mean, and the strikeout rate ticks up to 24.4% — so the on-base skills survive the translation better than the power does. Everything here hinges on whether the contact and speed hold as the pitching gets sharper, because if the BABIP compresses and the pop doesn't develop, what's left is a bench outfielder with a good eye rather than the everyday centerfielder the A+ surface suggests.

reports.name: Brandon Sproat
reports.published_report: The fastball at 96.7 mph is the one thing working in Sproat's favor, and the Statcast profile makes clear how much is riding on it. His chase rate sits at 25.5%, which is about as low as it gets, and when hitters aren't chasing, an 11.6% walk rate is what you get. The strikeout rate at 24.2% is league-average territory, not bad, but his xERA of 4.85 and a hard-hit rate of 43.1% say he's not missing barrels consistently enough to survive contact. If he ever finds a secondary offering that generates genuine swing-and-miss outside the zone, there's a functional back-end starter here; without it, the arm speed points toward a bullpen role and not much else.

reports.name: Anthony Solometo
reports.published_report:
Two innings. That's the honest anchor for everything that follows here — 2.0 IP at AA is a whisper, not a read, and the translation reflects it with low confidence attached to every number.

What's there isn't alarming but isn't loud either: the MLB-equivalent K/9 sits at 8.3 against a league context of 8.6, and the BB/9 translates to 3.5 where the average runs 3.2, leaving a K-BB% of 12.6% against a 13.5% baseline. Slightly below the line on every command-and-miss metric, which is a fine description of a depth arm ceiling. If the workload builds and the command tightens, you get a back-end guy who can eat innings at the big-league level; if it doesn't, this stays organizational filler. ValuCast has him sliding five spots in three days, and right now there's not enough sample to argue with the direction.

reports.name: Dylan Jordan
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is loud and the walk rate is the problem. Across A+ & A in 2026, Dylan Jordan has struck out 130 batters in 92 innings, a 12.7 K/9 that sits at the 92nd percentile of his pool, but the 4.5 BB/9 is barely league-middling, and when those two rates are forced to coexist the MLB-equivalent translation lands at a 12.2 K-BB%, right around a league-average 13.5. The whole profile hinges on whether he can tighten the zone enough to let the swing-and-miss actually carry value, because if the walks stay where they are, the strikeouts become noise rather than an advantage. Right now the ceiling and the floor are the same word: depth arm.

reports.name: Zac Thornton
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the thing to watch here. Across AAA & AA this season, Thornton has posted a 3.9 BB/9 over 62.7 innings, and when that translates to an MLB context it edges up to 3.7 while the league runs closer to 3.2. His strikeout translation lands at 8.3 K/9, just a tick below the MLB mean, which means the margin for error with runners on base is thin. The 4.0 ERA and 1.4 WHIP across AAA & AA aren't disqualifying, but the K-BB% translates to 12.0 where the league average sits at 13.5, so the profile reads as someone whose control needs to sharpen before the command catches up to the stuff. Left-handed depth arms can find roster spots on shape alone, but if the walk rate doesn't come down, that's the ceiling too.

reports.name: Brady Smith
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and the translation is where it gets complicated. Across A+ & A, Brady Smith is punching out hitters at 13.2 per nine over 80.7 innings, 118 strikeouts against 34 walks, and that K-BB% sits in the 94th percentile of the pitcher pool. The problem is that when you run the MLB-equivalent translation, the strikeouts flatten to 8.7 per nine, essentially league average, and the walks translate to 4.2 against a translated K-BB% of 13.1 percent where the MLB average sits at 13.5, meaning the dominant shape at the lower levels becomes a break-even profile one level at a time. The whole case hinges on whether the swing-and-miss travels up the ladder or belongs to the level.

reports.name: Marvin Alcantara
reports.published_report: The stolen bases are doing heavy lifting here. Fifteen at AA in 306 plate appearances is genuine production, but the rest of the offensive profile is thin enough that it can't carry the profile alone. His MLB-equivalent translation puts ISO at .119 where the average sits at .150, and his walk rate translates to 6.8% where the average sits at 8.5%, meaning the .238/.288/.368 AA line reflects a hitter who misses bats at a manageable rate but without the on-base skills or power to profile as more than a fringe regular. If the legs translate and the walk rate creeps up, he's a useful bench piece who gives a roster a specific skill; if neither develops, this is organizational depth at second base.

reports.published_report: The power profile at AA is the most interesting thing here, and also the thing that shrinks the most on translation. A .189 ISO across 293 PA at AA reads well on the card, but the MLB-equivalent drops to .146, roughly what a league-average bat produces, and the walk rate translates to 6.6% against a baseline that most big-league regulars clear comfortably. The contact side is quieter than the raw line suggests: a .277 BABIP holding up a .256 average, with 57 strikeouts kept manageable but an OBP of .302 that leaves almost no margin. If the power stays near that translated floor and the walk rate doesn't grow, what's left is a middle-infield profile that fits a bench role more than a lineup spot.

The MLB-equivalent translation puts his ISO at .133, a step below what an average big-league bat produces, so the gap-to-gap game isn't going to carry him; what keeps him relevant is the contact rate and the legs, a .266/.356 line in 364 AAA plate appearances built on 41 walks and a strikeout rate that translates just a tick above big-league norms. This profile hinges entirely on whether the speed plays at the next level, because if it doesn't, you're left with a below-average power bat and a walk rate that lands near the middle of the pack. Bench outfielder with a real path to a specific role if a team values defense and baserunning; organizational depth if they don't.
